summary.text: Lucas congruences show that for \(0\le m\le p-2\), splitting the defining sums for \(a(p+m)\) and \(c(p+m)\) at \(k=p\) produces two cancelling blocks, so all matrix entries past the anti-diagonal vanish modulo \(p\). At \(n=p-1\), \(\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k\) gives \(a(p-1)\equiv1\), while divisibility of the central binomial factors leaves only \(k=(p-1)/2\) in the second sum and gives \(c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\); multiplying the anti-diagonal entries by the reversal sign \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\) yields the two determinant congruences.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom nk^2
             \binom{2k}{k}\binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and put
\[
h=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
All congruences below are modulo \(p\).

We will first establish the binomial congruences needed in the proof, then prove the required vanishing and anti-diagonal evaluations for \(a\) and \(c\), and finally evaluate the two determinants.

### 1. Binomial congruences

We use Lucas's congruence in its recursive form
\[
\binom NK\equiv
\binom{N\bmod p}{K\bmod p}
\binom{\lfloor N/p\rfloor}{\lfloor K/p\rfloor}\pmod p.
\]
This follows, for example, by comparing coefficients in
\((1+x)^p\equiv 1+x^p\pmod p\), and iterating over the base-\(p\) digits.

In particular, if \(0\le m,k<p\), then
\[
\binom{p+m}{k}\equiv\binom mk                                      \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
\binom{p+m}{p+k}\equiv\binom mk.                                  \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, in (1) the leading base-\(p\) digit of \(k\) is zero, while in (2) both upper and lower leading digits are one.

We also need two facts about central binomial coefficients. If \(0\le r<p\) and \(p\le 2r\), then
\[
\binom{2r}{r}\equiv0.                                               \tag{3}
\]
To see this by Lucas's congruence, write \(2r=p+(2r-p)\). The low base-\(p\) digit of the upper argument is \(2r-p<r\), whereas the low digit of the lower argument is \(r\), so the corresponding digitwise binomial coefficient is zero.

For every \(0\le r<p\), we have
\[
\binom{2(p+r)}{p+r}\equiv 2\binom{2r}{r}.                           \tag{4}
\]
There are two cases. If \(2r<p\), the base-\(p\) digits of \(2(p+r)\) are \((2,2r)\), while those of \(p+r\) are \((1,r)\). Lucas's congruence therefore gives
\[
\binom{2(p+r)}{p+r}\equiv \binom21\binom{2r}{r}
=2\binom{2r}{r}.
\]
If \(2r\ge p\), then
\[
2(p+r)=3p+(2r-p).
\]
Lucas's congruence makes the left side of (4) zero because \(2r-p<r\). The right side is also zero by (3). Thus (4) holds in both cases.

Finally, for \(0\le k\le p-1\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k.                                        \tag{5}
\]
One proof is induction on \(k\). It is clear for \(k=0\). For \(k+1<p\), Pascal's identity gives
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}+\binom{p-1}{k+1}=\binom p{k+1}.
\]
The right side is divisible by \(p\), so
\(\binom{p-1}{k+1}\equiv-\binom{p-1}{k}\), proving (5).

### 2. Vanishing beyond the anti-diagonal

We claim that whenever
\[
0\le m\quad\text{and}\quad m+1<p,
\]
one has
\[
a(p+m)\equiv0                                                   \tag{6}
\]
and
\[
c(p+m)\equiv0.                                                  \tag{7}
\]

For (6), split the defining sum for \(a(p+m)\) into the ranges
\(0\le k<p\) and \(k=p+r\), \(0\le r\le m\). In the first range, (1) gives
\[
(-1)^k\binom{p+m}{k}^4
 \equiv (-1)^k\binom mk^4.
\]
When \(k>m\), this is zero. Thus the first range contributes exactly
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{m}(-1)^k\binom mk^4.
\]
In the second range, (2) and the oddness of \(p\) give
\[
(-1)^{p+r}\binom{p+m}{p+r}^4
\equiv -(-1)^r\binom mr^4.
\]
Consequently, the second range is the negative of the first, proving (6).

The proof of (7) is similar, but we keep track of the two central binomial coefficients. Define, for \(0\le k<p\),
\[
g(k)=2(-1)^k\binom mk^2
          \binom{2k}{k}\binom{2(m-k)}{m-k},
\]
with the understanding that this is zero when \(k>m\), since then \(\binom mk=0\).

Again split the sum defining \(c(p+m)\) into \(0\le k<p\) and \(k=p+r\), \(0\le r\le m\).

For the first range, if \(k>m\), both the original summand and \(g(k)\) are zero because (1) gives
\(\binom{p+m}{k}\equiv\binom mk=0\). If \(k\le m\), then
\[
p+m-k=p+(m-k),
\]
so (1) and (4) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(-1)^k\binom{p+m}{k}^2
  \binom{2k}{k}\binom{2(p+m-k)}{p+m-k}\\
&\qquad\equiv
2(-1)^k\binom mk^2
  \binom{2k}{k}\binom{2(m-k)}{m-k}
=g(k).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the first range contributes \(\sum_{k=0}^{m}g(k)\).

For the second range put \(k=p+r\), where \(0\le r\le m\). Then
\[
p+m-(p+r)=m-r.
\]
Using (2), (4), and \((-1)^{p+r}=-(-1)^r\), its summand is congruent to
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(-1)^{p+r}\binom{p+m}{p+r}^2
 \binom{2(p+r)}{p+r}\binom{2(m-r)}{m-r}\\
&\qquad\equiv
-2(-1)^r\binom mr^2
 \binom{2r}{r}\binom{2(m-r)}{m-r}
=-g(r).
\end{aligned}
\]
The two ranges therefore cancel term by term, proving (7).

### 3. The values on the anti-diagonal

We next evaluate \(a(p-1)\) and \(c(p-1)\) modulo \(p\).

Using (5),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4\\
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(p\) terms in this alternating sum, and \(p\) is odd, so
\[
a(p-1)\equiv1.                                                    \tag{8}
\]

For \(c(p-1)\), we show that all terms except the middle term \(k=h\) vanish. Recall that \(p-1=2h\).

If \(k<h\), put \(r=p-1-k\). Then \(r<p\) and \(2r\ge p\), so by (3)
\[
\binom{2(p-1-k)}{p-1-k}=\binom{2r}{r}\equiv0.
\]
Thus the summand vanishes.

If \(k>h\), then \(k<p\) and \(2k\ge p\), so (3) gives
\[
\binom{2k}{k}\equiv0.
\]
Thus this summand also vanishes.

Only \(k=h\) remains. Since \(p-1-h=h\) and \(2h=p-1\), all three binomial expressions occurring in this summand are \(\binom{p-1}{h}\), with the first one squared. Hence (5) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
c(p-1)
&\equiv (-1)^h
 \binom{p-1}{h}^2
 \binom{p-1}{h}
 \binom{p-1}{h}\\
&\equiv (-1)^h\bigl((-1)^h\bigr)^4
=(-1)^h.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^h.                                               \tag{9}
\]

### 4. An anti-triangular determinant formula

Let \(M=(M_{ij})_{0\le i,j<p}\) be a matrix over any commutative ring such that
\[
M_{ij}=0\qquad\text{whenever }i+j\ge p.                            \tag{10}
\]
Reverse the order of its columns, forming
\[
B_{ij}=M_{i,p-1-j}.
\]
If \(i>j\), then
\[
i+(p-1-j)\ge p,
\]
so (10) gives \(B_{ij}=0\). Thus \(B\) is upper triangular, and
\[
\det B=\prod_{i=0}^{p-1}M_{i,p-1-i}.                               \tag{11}
\]
The reversal permutation has one inversion for every pair of distinct positions, hence \(\binom p2\) inversions and sign
\[
(-1)^{\binom p2}.
\]
Reversing the columns multiplies the determinant by this sign. Since this sign is its own inverse, (11) yields
\[
\det M=(-1)^{\binom p2}
       \prod_{i=0}^{p-1}M_{i,p-1-i}.                               \tag{12}
\]
Because \(p=2h+1\),
\[
\binom p2=\frac{p(p-1)}2=ph.
\]
As \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{\binom p2}=(-1)^{ph}=(-1)^h.                                \tag{13}
\]

### 5. Evaluation of the two determinants

Let
\[
A=(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p},\qquad
C=(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
We reduce their entries modulo \(p\). Reduction modulo \(p\) commutes with determinants because the determinant is an integer polynomial in the matrix entries.

Suppose \(0\le i,j<p\) and \(i+j\ge p\). Write
\[
i+j=p+m,
\qquad m=i+j-p.
\]
Since \(i,j\le p-1\), we have \(i+j\le2p-2\), and therefore
\[
0\le m\le p-2,
\qquad m+1<p.
\]
It follows from (6) and (7) that
\[
a(i+j)\equiv0,
\qquad c(i+j)\equiv0.
\]
Thus both reduced matrices satisfy the hypothesis of the anti-triangular determinant formula (12).

On the anti-diagonal, \(j=p-1-i\), so every entry of the reduced matrix \(A\) equals \(a(p-1)\), while every entry of the reduced matrix \(C\) equals \(c(p-1)\). Consequently, (12), (13), (8), and (9) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det A
&\equiv (-1)^h\prod_{i=0}^{p-1}a(p-1)\\
&=(-1)^h a(p-1)^p\\
&\equiv(-1)^h.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the first asserted congruence.

Similarly,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det C
&\equiv(-1)^h\prod_{i=0}^{p-1}c(p-1)\\
&=(-1)^h c(p-1)^p\\
&\equiv(-1)^h\bigl((-1)^h\bigr)^p.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(p\) is odd, \(\bigl((-1)^h\bigr)^p=(-1)^h\). Hence
\[
\det C\equiv(-1)^h(-1)^h=1.
\]

Recalling that \(h=(p-1)/2\), we have proved
\[
\boxed{\det(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\det(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv1\pmod p}.
\]
